title: The Order of the Temple as a transfer network, from the founding to the suppression
register: documentary, the ledger is the argument
summary: A pilgrim deposited silver in one house and drew it in another against a letter, so the money travelled as writing while the metal stayed put. The network that carried it was a religious order with houses from the Atlantic to the Jordan, fed by manors and vineyards along the Rhine, and it ended by decree in 1312 rather than by decline.

nodes.name: Jerusalem
nodes.note: The quarters on the Temple Mount that named the order. Lost with the kingdom after Hattin in 1187.

nodes.name: Acre
nodes.note: Headquarters after the recovery of the city in 1191, and the fortified port of debarkation for the eastern trade. Fell in the siege of 1291.

nodes.name: Paris, Maison du Temple
nodes.note: The enclosure north of the walls. By the end of the twelfth century it held the royal treasury, and by the end of the thirteenth its keep stored the treasure of the king of France alongside the order's own.

nodes.name: London, New Temple
nodes.note: Consecrated in 1185, replacing the Old Temple in Holborn. It acted as the royal treasury: 500 marks lodged for the Poitou expedition in 1221, the king's wardrobe kept there in 1225, and it is named a royal treasury in 1274 and 1276.

nodes.name: Tomar
nodes.note: Founded in March 1160 as the order's Portuguese headquarters, the first castle laid out for that purpose. Its estates passed to the Order of Christ rather than to the Hospital.

nodes.name: La Rochelle
nodes.note: The Atlantic outlet, used mainly for shipping wine and produce. The preceptory entrance survives on the Rue des Templiers.

nodes.name: Marseille
nodes.note: One of the two ports most used for passage to the East, carrying pilgrims and specie toward Acre.

nodes.name: Barcelona
nodes.note: The other principal port of embarkation for the East, and the maritime end of the Aragonese houses.

nodes.name: Limassol
nodes.note: The headquarters after Acre fell, held by Jacques de Molay. The last seat of the order before the arrests.

nodes.name: Monzón
nodes.note: The Aragonese stronghold, granted in the settlement of 1143. Its estates went to the Order of Montesa because the king of Aragon refused the transfer to the Hospital.

nodes.name: The Order of the Temple
nodes.note: The corporate person that made the network one network. Recognised at the Council of Troyes in 1129 and privileged by Omne Datum Optimum in 1139, which exempted it from local jurisdiction and let a single rule bind houses in different kingdoms. Dissolved by Vox in excelso in 1312.

nodes.name: The Templar fleet
nodes.note: The shipping arm that carried pilgrims, bullion and grain. No fixed locus, so it is tethered to the ports it worked.

nodes.name: Crown of France
nodes.note: Depositor at Paris from Philip Augustus onward, and in 1307 the party that arrested its own bankers.

nodes.name: Crown of England
nodes.note: Depositor at the New Temple. The 1221 Poitou instalment is among the earliest documented deposits.

nodes.name: Paris Temple treasury
nodes.note: The vault in the keep. It held the order's treasure and the king's in the same walls, which is why the seizure of one was the seizure of the other.

nodes.name: New Temple treasury
nodes.note: Named as a royal treasury in 1274 and 1276, and holding royal funds from 1221.

nodes.name: Mainz, Templerhof
nodes.note: The regional court for the Rhenish holdings, an agrarian and viticultural footprint rather than a fortress, from the middle of the twelfth century.

nodes.name: Klein-Winternheim
nodes.note: A grange and vineyard holding south of Mainz. The order's wealth here was grown, not deposited.

nodes.name: Rötgen, Rheingau
nodes.note: An estate and vineyard on the right bank, named in Addison's roll of Rhenish holdings. The estate is attested; the exact locus is not, so it is placed in the Rheingau generally rather than pinned to a point.

nodes.name: Boppard, Templerhaus
nodes.note: A fortified court in the gorge. The stone house survives, first mentioned in 1234 and built between about 1200 and 1240 in late Romanesque. The building and its date are firm; the Templar attribution is traditional rather than documented, and the name it carries is the tradition.

nodes.name: Nürburg
nodes.note: Named among the Rhenish assets in the territorial rolls. The reference is a listing rather than a description, so little beyond the name is claimed here.

nodes.name: Chateau Pelerin
nodes.note: Built in 1218 on a promontory the sea guarded on three sides, and never taken by assault. It was evacuated on 14 August 1291, the last mainland holding the order gave up.

nodes.name: Safed
nodes.note: The great castle of upper Galilee, taken by Baibars in 1266 when he completed his conquest of the region.

nodes.name: Tortosa
nodes.note: The northern stronghold on the Syrian coast. Evacuated on 3 August 1291.

nodes.name: Sidon
nodes.note: Evacuated on 14 July 1291, the first of the coastal houses to go in that summer.

nodes.name: Baghras
nodes.note: The castle guarding the Belen pass into Antioch, held until Baibars took it in 1268.

nodes.name: Gaza
nodes.note: Granted to the order in the middle of the twelfth century as the southern march toward Egypt. Lost with the kingdom in 1187.

nodes.name: Ruad
nodes.note: A rock off Tortosa held after everything on the mainland was gone. Its loss in 1302 ended the crusader presence entirely, ten years before the order itself.

nodes.name: Provins
nodes.note: A fair town, and on its Rue des Changes the order issued credit notes to travellers who would need ready money on reaching Jerusalem. The house itself was not founded until 1193.

nodes.name: Troyes
nodes.note: Where the council of 1129 recognised the order and its rule was written down. Also a fair town, so the place that made the order legitimate was also a place that cleared payments.

nodes.name: Bar-sur-Aube
nodes.note: One of the four fair towns whose cycle ran the year.

nodes.name: Lagny-sur-Marne
nodes.note: The fourth fair town, closest to Paris.

nodes.name: Payns
nodes.note: The seat of Hugues de Payns, born here about 1070, who founded the order. A village of some hundreds of people at the root of a network that reached the Jordan.

nodes.name: Richerenches
nodes.note: Founded in 1136 on land given by Hugues de Bourbouton, the order's first great agricultural house. By 1138 it supervised the other Provencal houses: cereals, vineyards, mills, sheep for wool, and war horses.

nodes.name: Douzens
nodes.note: An early Languedoc holding, farmed rather than garrisoned.

nodes.name: Cressing Temple
nodes.note: The earliest English holding, granted in 1137. Its two enormous barns still stand, which is the plainest surviving statement of what the order's wealth rested on.

nodes.name: Temple Bruer
nodes.note: One of the largest English preceptories, on the heath.

nodes.name: Garway
nodes.note: A round church on the Welsh march, its plan copied from the Holy Sepulchre.

nodes.name: Balantrodoch
nodes.note: The Scottish headquarters, granted by David I. The village still carries the name Temple.

nodes.name: Clontarf
nodes.note: The Irish headquarters, on the bay north of Dublin.

nodes.name: Soure
nodes.note: Received and rebuilt in March 1128, the order's first castle anywhere.

nodes.name: Almourol
nodes.note: A castle on an island in the Tagus, guarding the river frontier.

nodes.name: Miravet
nodes.note: Above the Ebro. In 1307 the Aragonese brothers shut themselves in here and held out for more than a year rather than submit to arrest.

nodes.name: Gardeny
nodes.note: Granted after the taking of Lleida in 1149.

nodes.name: Penyiscola
nodes.note: A late acquisition on a rock in the sea, held only eighteen years.

nodes.name: Ponferrada
nodes.note: On the pilgrim road to Compostela, guarding the crossing.

nodes.name: Jerez de los Caballeros
nodes.note: The knights in the town's name are these ones.

nodes.name: Rome, Santa Maria dell'Aventino
nodes.note: The order's Roman house, close to the power that both privileged it and dissolved it.

nodes.name: Genoa
nodes.note: A maritime republic whose ships the order used and competed with.

nodes.name: Brindisi
nodes.note: The heel of Italy, the shortest crossing to the East and a standing embarkation port for the crusades.

nodes.name: Barletta
nodes.note: The order's Apulian centre, provisioning the eastern passage with grain.

nodes.name: Tempelhof
nodes.note: The order's holding in the Brandenburg march. The name outlived it by seven hundred years and ended up on an airfield.

nodes.name: Chwarszczany
nodes.note: The eastern edge of the order's reach, a chapel still standing on the Oder plain.

nodes.name: Bruges
nodes.note: Where the wool money was, and the northern counterpart to the Champagne clearing.

nodes.name: Vrana
nodes.note: The Dalmatian house, on the coast road between the Latin west and Byzantium.

nodes.name: Bordeaux
nodes.note: The wine port of the English crown's French lands.

nodes.name: The Champagne fair cycle
nodes.note: Not a place but a calendar: six fairs a year rotating between Lagny, Bar-sur-Aube, Provins and Troyes, so that the clearing house was a date rather than a building. Debts contracted at one fair were settled at the next.

nodes.name: The Papacy
nodes.note: Recognised the order at Troyes in 1129, exempted it from every local jurisdiction by Omne Datum Optimum in 1139, and dissolved it by Vox in excelso in 1312. The same party made the network possible and ended it.

nodes.name: Arles
nodes.note: On the Rhone delta, the road between the Provencal farms and the sea.
